author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will walk, with the rest of your division, to the village of Cbafà-A'nn-, where it is said that there are 200 camels belonging to Djezzar, grains and sheep. The chief authorising officer gives an instruction to the commissioner of your division to. take all these objects."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: To General Lawes: You will walk, with the rest of your division, to the village of Cbafà-A'nn-, where it is said that there are 200 camels belonging to Djezzar, grains and sheep.
tweet: I want your division to investigate the reported camels, grain, and sheep near the village, and have the authorized officer arrange their collection.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Commander Lambert will see the authorising officer, who will send a convoy to Hayfà tonight, and General Dommartiu"
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: To Chief Of Escadrox Lambert: The Commander Lambert will see the authorising officer, who will send a convoy to Hayfà tonight, and General Dommartiu.
tweet: I direct Lambert to meet the authorizing officer and arrange a convoy to Haifa tonight.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That it is not our practice to come before seven o'clock in the morning, and that I know that the great heat keeps them from coming after."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: To Al: Citovex Folhikk: That it is not our practice to come before seven o'clock in the morning, and that I know that the great heat keeps them from coming after.
tweet: I explain that we do not arrive before seven in the morning, and the heat keeps them from coming later.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The provinces of Fayoum, Minyeh and Beny-Soueyf, General Citizen, have never had to provide for the needs of your division, since even the administration has not been entrusted to you. Please do not interfere in any way with the administration of these provinces."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Cairo. To Al-Gexeral Desaix: The provinces of Fayoum, Minyeh and Beny-Soueyf, General Citizen, have never had to provide for the needs of your division…
voice: @desaix The provinces of Fayoum, Minyeh and Beny-Soueyf, General Citizen, have never had to provide for the needs of your division, since even the administration has not been entrusted to you
tweet: I have not assigned Fayoum, Minyeh, or Beny-Soueyf to your division. Leave their administration alone; it is not yours to direct.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You are not subject in any way, Citizen General, to General Desaix for the administration of the province. You will regard as null all the orders he would give you on this subject."
sourceTitle: To At Gkxeral Za. Ionchek, Cairo, 1790-08-17
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Cairo. To At Gkxeral Za. Ionchek: You are not subject in any way, Citizen General, to General Desaix for the administration of the province.
voice: @ionchek You are not subject in any way, Citizen General, to General Desaix for the administration of the province
tweet: You answer to no one but me in the administration of this province. Treat any contrary orders from Desaix as void.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “From Bonifacio to Cape Corse, from Ajaccio to Bastia, nothing rises but a chorus of curses against you. Your friends hide, your kin disown you. […]”
sourceTitle: Letter to Matteo Buttafoco, deputy of Corsica, January 1791
archive: Masson & Schütz, Napoléon manuscrits inédits 1786–1791 (Paris, 1908) — public domain (French)
context: The 21-year-old denounces Corsica's deputy: treason itemized in letters of blood. Dated by the edition. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Depuis Bonifacio au cap Corse, depuis Ajaccio à Bastia, ce n'est qu'un chorus d'imprécations contre vous. Vos amis se cachent, vos parents vous désavouent.
tweet: From Bonifacio to Cape Corse, from Ajaccio to Bastia, nothing rises but a chorus of curses against you. Your friends hide, your kin disown you. You have ruined Corsica; you have sold its honour to the French.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Articlk l — The town of Ancona and the villages that depend on it will be administered by a municipality composed of fifteen members."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Articlk l — The town of Ancona and the villages that depend on it will be administered by a municipality composed of fifteen members.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Chief General is instructing me to ask you, gentlemen, that he give orders that there be no hostility against the Republic of Venice for four days, starting tomorrow."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: To And Leoxardo Giustixiaxi: The Chief General is instructing me to ask you, gentlemen, that he give orders that there be no hostility against the Republic of Venice for four days, starting tomorrow.
voice: @giustixiaxi The Chief General is instructing me to ask you, gentlemen, that he give orders that there be no hostility against the Republic of Venice for four days, starting tomorrow
tweet: I have asked for a four-day halt to hostilities with Venice, beginning tomorrow. Please have the necessary orders issued.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You have three goals to fulfill: 1° Xe leave nothing that can be useful to the Emperor and promote the recovery of a military navy; "2° Make go to France anything that can be useful to the Navy;"
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Passariano. To Citizen Citytard: You have three goals to fulfill: 1° Xe leave nothing that can be useful to the Emperor and promote the recovery of a military navy.
tweet: I set two goals: deny the Emperor anything useful and send France whatever can help restore its navy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “However, I send you 20 saddles which I ask you to return to the store, when you have received those to the regiment. Do not waste a moment, please, to organize your province, to mount your disembarkations."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Cairo. To General Mirat: However, I send you 20 saddles which I ask you to return to the store, when you have received those to the regiment.
voice: @mirat Do not waste a moment, please, to organize your province, to mount your disembarkations
tweet: I have sent twenty saddles back to the stores. Organize the province and prepare the landings without delay.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received all the various letters you wrote me. Here we are still much in the same position. The army is thirty thousand strong. We have eleven batteries against Fort Malbousquet. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Toulon eve: thirty thousand men, eleven batteries, and a stolen battery retaken. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu toutes les différentes lettres que vous m'avez écrites. Ici nous sommes toujours à peu près dans la même position. L'armée est forte de trente mille hommes. Nous avons onze batteries contre le fort de Malbousquet.
tweet: I have received your letters. We remain in much the same position, with 30,000 troops and eleven batteries against Fort Malbousquet. The siege continues.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I promised you brilliant successes, and you see I keep my word. Worn out with fatigue and work, I could not tell you first; suffice it that the English carried off none of our guns. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Toulon retaken: 'I promised you brilliant successes, and you see I keep my word.' Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je t'avais annoncé de brillants succès, et tu vois que je te tiens parole. Excédé de fatigue et d'occupation, je n'ai pas pu t'en instruire le premier; il me suffira de te dire que les Anglais n'ont enlevé aucune de nos pièces.
tweet: I promised you brilliant successes, and you see I keep my word. Worn out with fatigue and work, I could not tell you first; suffice it that the English carried off none of our guns. The defence holds firm.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Fort Saint-Nicolas cannot withstand a quarter-hour. The three walls closing it town-side are razed. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Saint-Nicolas untenable: three enceintes razed, open on all sides. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le fort Saint-Nicolas n'est pas susceptible d'un quart d'heure de défense. Les trois enceintes qui fermaient le fort du côté de la ville ont été démolies.
tweet: Fort Saint-Nicolas cannot withstand a quarter-hour. The three walls closing it town-side are razed. I am pushing the works forward with all speed. The enemy will find no shelter there.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “More grain ships came into the roads this evening; but the enemy squadron keeps them from venturing through. I shall have two batteries built which, once finished, will make coastal traffic safe, under the very eyes of the enemy squadron. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Committee of Public Safety, 1794-02-28
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Coast guns: grain ships, English squadrons, and two new batteries. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est encore arrivé ce soir des bâtiments chargés de blé dans cette rade; mais l'escadre ennemie les empêche de se hasarder à passer. Je vais faire établir deux batteries, qui, dès qu'elles seront achevées, rendront le cabotage de la côte sûr, à la vue même de l'escadre ennemie.
tweet: More grain ships came into the roads this evening; but the enemy squadron keeps them from venturing through. I shall have two batteries built which, once finished, will make coastal traffic safe, under the very eyes of the enemy squadron.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I will have two batteries established, which, as soon as they are completed, will render the coasting of the coast on, in the sight of the enemy wing."
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Thirty thousand men, eleven batteries: the gunner's apprenticeship, in French. To Citizen Maygxet: I will have two batteries established, which, as soon as they are completed, will render the coasting of the coast on, in the sight of the enemy wing.
voice: I will have two batteries established, which, as soon as they are completed, will render the coasting of the coast on, in the sight of the enemy wing
tweet: I am setting up two batteries where the enemy can see them. Once they are ready, they should make the coast untenable for the opposing wing.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Rebuild Sainte-Marguerite point battery; raise the mortar parapet eight feet. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Sainte-Marguerite battery rebuilt, mortars raised eight feet. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il faut rétablir la batterie de la pointe de l'île Sainte-Marguerite; il faut élever de huit pieds l'épaulement des mortiers.
tweet: I order: Rebuild Sainte-Marguerite point battery; raise the mortar parapet eight feet. The works must be completed before the enemy can react. Speed is everything in these preparations.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Piedmont's plain demands superior force; join the Alps and Italy armies for it. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: No Piedmont plain without superior force: join Alps and Italy armies. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: L'on ne peut se présenter dans la plaine de Piémont qu'avec des forces supérieures à son ennemi; pour obtenir cette supériorité il faut réunir l'armée des Alpes et celle d'Italie.
tweet: I say: Piedmont plain demands superior force; join the Alps and Italy armies for it. A divided command will fail; unity of effort is the only path to victory in that theatre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “1. Secure rearwards against enemies within and without. 2. Unite the Alps and Italy defence systems. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Secure rearwards first, unite Alps-Italy defence. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: 1° Assurer ses derrières, soit contre les ennemis internes, soit contre les ennemis externes. 2° Réunir le système de défense des armées des Alpes et d'Italie.
tweet: I set the plan: 1. Secure rearwards against enemies within and without. 2. Unite the Alps and Italy defence systems. 3. Concentrate artillery where it can strike the decisive blow. These are the pillars.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Call it not Pelletier but Marguerite island; renaming places needs a Convention decree. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Marguerite not Pelletier: island names need a Convention decree. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Tu ne dois pas appeler l'île Sainte-Marguerite l'île Pelletier. Il faut un décret de la Convention pour pouvoir changer le nom des places.
tweet: Call it not Pelletier but Marguerite island; renaming places needs a Convention decree. I insist on the proper forms; revolutionary nomenclature must follow the law.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Republic breeds two alarmists: grain-famine criers and powder-fearers. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Two alarmist breeds: grain-famine criers and powder-fearers. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il y a dans la République deux espèces d'alarmistes, ceux qui crient famine de grain et ceux qui ont toujours peur de rester sans poudre.
tweet: The Republic breeds two alarmists: grain-famine criers and powder-fearers. Both spread panic to serve their own ends. I will not tolerate defeatism disguised as caution.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is imposture to claim 28 thousand powder at Antibes when you hold 45. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Powder imposture: 45 not 28 thousand at Antibes. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: C'est une imposture de dire que tu n'as que 28 milliers de poudre à Antibes, lorsque tu en as 45 milliers.
tweet: It is imposture to claim 28 thousand powder at Antibes when you hold 45. I know the true state of the magazines; false returns will be punished severely.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I wrote you several times unanswered; I cannot think it contempt. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Unanswered letters, but no contempt: the Corsican affair. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je t'ai écrit plusieurs fois, mais tu ne m'as pas répondu; je ne puis penser que ce soit par mépris.
tweet: I wrote you several times unanswered; I cannot think it contempt. Perhaps my letters miscarried, but silence from a subordinate is not acceptable. Respond at once.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I intend to use all haste with the commissions for your wife. Desiree demands my portrait; you will give it to her should she still wish for it; this not being the case, keep it for yourself. […]”
sourceTitle: To Joseph Buonaparte, Prairial 1795 (revolutionary date; day approximate)
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Prairial Year III: Désirée demands his portrait. Revolutionary calendar date; rendered to the 1st, marked approximate.
tweet: I intend to use all haste with the commissions for your wife. Desiree demands my portrait; you will give it to her should she still wish for it; if not, keep it for yourself. Family matters must not distract from duty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Never take me for a dupe; these twenty days I know Saliceti hides with you. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Saliceti hides at her house, twenty days known. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je n'ai jamais voulu être pris pour dupe; je sais, depuis plus de vingt jours, que Saliceti est caché chez vous.
tweet: Never take me for a dupe; these twenty days I know Saliceti hides with you. I see through the manoeuvres of those who think themselves clever. The truth will out.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your No. 16 received. Chiappe's letter pleased me. I shall do what I can for Lucien. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Chiappe pleases; Lucien to be placed; letter No. 16 received. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu ta lettre numérotée 16. La lettre de Chiappe m'a fait plaisir. Je ferai ce que je pourrai pour placer Lucien.
tweet: Your No. 16 received. Chiappe's letter pleased me. I shall do what I can for Lucien. Brother, your requests find a willing ear when they serve the cause.

context: To his brother Joseph: Salutations to your wife. I should much like to embrace her in Paris, where one is better than at Genoa.
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Salutations to your wife. I should much like to embrace her in Paris, where one is better than at Genoa. It is here that an upright and prudent man, who confines himself to his friends, lives with all the liberty imaginable, if he wishes, and is perfectly free. […]”
voice: I should much like to embrace her in Paris, where one is better than at Genoa
tweet: Still no letter — a month since you left. Louis studies mathematics at Châlons; Junot lives large on his father money. I wait your word before buying property — nothing suitable under 800,000 francs. Embrace your wife for me in Paris, where one lives freer than Genoa.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am a General employed in the army of the West; my malady detains me here. I await further details from you. I believe you avoid speaking to me about Desire on purpose, &c.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Unemployed general, sick in Paris, awaiting fate.
tweet: I am a general employed in the army of the West; my malady detains me here. I await further details from you. I believe you avoid speaking to me about Desiree on purpose.

context: Paris. To his brother Joseph: Carriages and fashionables have reappeared, and forget, or rather only remember as a dream, that they ever ceased to shine.
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There was an immense crowd at the doors from 2 P.M., although prices had been trebled. Carriages and fashionables have reappeared, and forget, or rather only remember as a dream, that they ever ceased to shine. […]”
tweet: I report good news on every front: the English re-embark, Pichegru crosses the Rhine, the Vendée is quiet, Spain nears peace. And Paris drowns in pleasure — opera crowds at triple prices, fashion back as if the Terror were a dream.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The English must re-embark within days. Pichegru prepares the Rhine crossing. The Vendée proper is quiet. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: English re-embarking soon; Pichegru prepares the Rhine; Vendée quiet. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les Anglais seront obligés de s'embarquer sous peu de jours. Pichegru prépare le passage du Rhin. La Vendée proprement dite est tranquille.
tweet: I say the English must re-embark within days. Pichegru prepares the Rhine crossing. The Vendée is quiet. The Chouans only north of the Loire. Peace with Spain is imminent.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The English will be obliged to re-embark in a few days. Pichegru is preparing to pass the Rhine. La Vendee is tranquil, and the Chouans are only seen north of the Loire. Peace with Spain is imminent. " The Dutch appear warm friends of their Revolution. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Quiberon landings; Pichegru about to cross the Rhine.
tweet: I report: English will re-embark in days. Pichegru prepares Rhine crossing. La Vendee tranquil, Chouans only north of Loire. Peace with Spain imminent. Dutch warm friends of Revolution. Italy grows rich on France spoils. Luxury and arts flourish astonishingly.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I did not write, friend, for I had no pleasant news to give. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: No pleasant news: unfrocked war commissary, departure pending. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je ne vous ai pas écrit, mon ami, parce que je n'avais aucune nouvelle agréable à vous donner.
tweet: I did not write, friend, for I had no pleasant news to give. Silence is sometimes the only honest report when affairs go ill.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I did not write to you, my friend, because I had no good news to give you. You are not kept war commissioner;"
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Paris. To Citizen Lioinod: I did not write to you, my friend, because I had no good news to give you.
voice: @lioinod I did not write to you, my friend, because I had no good news to give you
tweet: I stayed silent because I had no good news for you, my friend. I did not want to write merely to disappoint you.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Twelve thousand émigrés landed at Quiberon, battering the isthmus passage. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Twelve thousand émigrés landed; English ships hold the isthmus. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les émigrés, au nombre de douze mille, étant débarqués dans la presqu'île de Quiberon, avaient établi des batteries pour défendre le passage de l'isthme.
tweet: Twelve thousand émigrés landed at Quiberon, battering the isthmus passage. The Royalist invasion has begun; we must crush it before it spreads.

context: To Commissary Sucy: I retire satisfied that the injustice done to the service will be sufficiently felt by those who know how to appreciate matters.
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I retire satisfied that the injustice done to the service will be sufficiently felt by those who know how to appreciate matters. […]”
voice: I retire satisfied that the injustice done to the service will be sufficiently felt by those who know how to appreciate matters
tweet: I refuse the Vendée — others command brigades better than I, but none serves guns like me. Let the injustice sting those who understand service. Health, constancy, never discouraged.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I congratulate you on joining the army Fortune, favour, and the esteem of men vary and oscillate perpetually I have been appointed to serve in the army of La Vendee as General of the Line: I have not accepted, A great many ofificers would command a brigade better than I could; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Fortune varies: angling for employment.
tweet: I congratulate you on joining the army. Fortune, favour, esteem of men vary perpetually. I have been appointed general of the Line in La Vendee: I have not accepted. Many would command a brigade better; few command artillery so well.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Committee sent you, General, by last courier, Italy's direction instructions. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Italy instructions via last courier: reinforcements coming. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le Comité de salut public vous a fait passer, Général, par le dernier courrier, des instructions relatives à la direction de l'armée d'Italie.
tweet: The Committee sent you, general, by last courier, Italy's direction instructions. You will execute them without delay. The army of Italy awaits your orders.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I hope you will have a consulate in the kingdom of Naples, at peace with that power. All is very quiet here. A third of the Convention is about to be renewed. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Bureaucrat in Paris: Naples consulships hoped, Convention thirds renewed. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'espère que tu auras un consulat dans le royaume de Naples, à la paix avec cette puissance. L'on est ici fort tranquille. L'on va renouveler le tiers de la Convention.
tweet: I hope you will have a consulate in the kingdom of Naples, at peace with that power. All is very quiet here. A third of the Convention is about to be renewed. The political winds shift but we hold our course.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We forward, General, a note just received from Switzerland. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Incoming voice: Swiss note examined; enemy conforms to true interest. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Nous vous faisons passer, Général, une note qui nous a été envoyée de Suisse.
tweet: We forward, general, a note just received from Switzerland. The diplomatic channels remain open; intelligence flows through them.

context: Paris, sick and scheming, weeks before Vendémiaire. To his brother Joseph: Kellermann to that of the Alps; Hoche has been transferred to La Vendee.
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Royalists are stirring; we shall see how this will end Scherer has gone to the army of Italy; Kellermann to that of the Alps; Hoche has been transferred to La Vendee; […]”
tweet: The Royalists stir — we shall see. Schérer goes to Italy, Kellermann to the Alps, Hoche to Vendée. The Committee keeps me in guns, likely at Paris — and I may be seized with the madness of marrying. Speak to Désirée brother for me.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Committee thinks I cannot leave France while war lasts. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vol. I — public domain (French)
context: Cannot leave France while war lasts; artillery restoration likely. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le Comité a pensé qu'il était impossible que je sortisse de France tant que durera la guerre.
tweet: The Committee thinks I cannot leave France while war lasts. They are right; my place is with the army, not in the chambers of politicians.

context: Paris, sick and scheming, weeks before Vendémiaire. To his brother Joseph: I am going to write to your wife. I am well satisfied with Louis; he answers the hopes 1 conceived of him.
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to write to your wife. I am well satisfied with Louis; he answers the hopes 1 conceived of him. He is E 2 a good fellow after my fashion — zvarmth, wit, talent honesty, goodness, all coinbined. […]”
tweet: Fear nothing for me — I have friends in every party. Louis answers all my hopes: warmth, wit, talent, honesty, all combined. I live only for my family pleasure; keep luck with me and I shall fulfill all your desires.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “No matter what happens, you need feel no alarm concerning me, as I have for friends the best men of all parties. Mariette is extremely zealous in my behalf: you are aware of his opinions. I am on intimate terms with Doulcet You know my other friends of an opposite opinion. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Convention renewed; Vendémiaire brewing.
tweet: No matter what, you need feel no alarm for me; I have friends among the best men of all parties. Mariette is zealous for me; you know his opinions. I am intimate with Doulcet. You know my friends of opposite opinion. I will write your wife.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
